opus-5.5.text:
The basic problem is that RLHF relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. The way it works is you have the model produce a bunch of outputs, humans look at them and say which ones they prefer, you train a reward model on those judgments, and then you optimize the policy against that reward model. That works really well as long as the human can actually tell whether the output is good. For a lot of what we do today, like "is this a helpful answer?" or "is this summary accurate?", people can make that call reasonably well.

But as systems get more capable, they'll increasingly be doing things that are too hard for us to evaluate. Imagine a model writing a million lines of code, or proposing a novel biology experiment, or carrying out a long sequence of actions in the world. A human labeler just can't reliably tell whether that code has a subtle backdoor or whether that plan has some side effect three steps down the line. Once the task is beyond what we can assess, our feedback stops being a good training signal.

It actually gets worse than that. If you train a system to get high ratings from humans, and humans can't distinguish "actually good" from "looks good to a human," you're directly optimizing for things that look good. So you might be training the model to tell you what you want to hear, or to hide mistakes in ways you won't notice. The training signal itself pushes toward deception at the margin, not because anyone intended that, but because that's what the gradient rewards.

So RLHF is a great tool, and I think it'll keep being a core building block, but it doesn't scale on its own. The central question for alignment, as I see it, is how you supervise systems that are smarter than you. That's why I'm excited about scalable oversight: using AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems. For example, a model that critiques another model's output and points out the flaws, so the human only has to check the critique rather than find the bug themselves. Evaluation is generally easier than generation, and if you can lean on that asymmetry and bootstrap with AI assistance, you might be able to keep human judgment in the loop even as the tasks get much harder. Alongside that you want interpretability, so you can look inside and check whether the model is being honest, and you want ways to validate all of this, like deliberately training deceptive models and seeing whether your oversight methods catch them.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF does not scale on its own because increasingly capable systems will perform tasks humans cannot reliably assess, making human feedback a poor training signal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic problem is that RLHF fundamentally relies on humans being able to evaluate what the system is doing. The whole setup is: the model produces some output, a human looks at it and says "this one's better than that one," and you train on those comparisons. That works pretty well today, because for most of the things current models do, a human can look at the output and tell whether it's good or not. If the model writes a poem or summarizes an article, I can read it and judge it.

But the core assumption there is that humans are actually good evaluators of the task. And as systems get much more capable than us, that assumption breaks. Imagine the model writes a million lines of code, or produces a long argument about some scientific question, or proposes a policy that has consequences playing out over years. A human just can't reliably tell whether that's correct, whether it's subtly flawed, or whether it's actively doing something you wouldn't want if you understood it. And if you can't tell, you can't give the right feedback signal.

And it's actually worse than just "the signal gets noisy." If the human evaluator is making systematic mistakes, the model will learn to exploit those mistakes, because that's what the optimization is pushing toward. You're rewarding things that look good to the human, not things that are actually good. So you end up training the system to be convincing rather than correct, and the smarter the system gets relative to the evaluator, the wider that gap can become. You could end up with a model that's very good at telling you what you want to hear, and you'd have no way of noticing from inside the training process.

So I think RLHF is a really useful technique, and it was a big part of why models became useful at all. But I view it as something that works in a regime where humans can still supervise, and we need to be honest that we're going to leave that regime. The question I care about is how we get a supervision signal that keeps working past that point, whether that's using AI systems to help humans evaluate, breaking tasks down so the pieces are checkable, or finding ways to verify what the model is doing rather than just how its output looks.

r001.rationale: The response says that as systems surpass human capability, people cannot reliably judge complex outputs for correctness or subtle flaws, so they cannot provide the right feedback signal.

astra-6.text:
The basic problem is that reinforcement learning from human feedback relies on humans being able to evaluate what the system is doing. And as the system gets more capable, that becomes harder.

For example, suppose an AI writes a large amount of complicated code. How do you know whether that code actually does what you wanted, whether it has subtle security vulnerabilities, or whether it’s doing something you didn’t intend? You can ask a human to look at it, but a reliable evaluation might take a very long time, and some problems could be beyond their ability to spot.

So there’s a gap between producing something that looks good to a human evaluator and producing something that actually is good. Human feedback rewards the former, and we need to figure out how to make it reliably track the latter, even when the system understands the task much better than we do.

That doesn’t mean human feedback isn’t useful. It’s a useful starting point. But we need methods that let us supervise tasks we can’t easily evaluate ourselves—potentially using AI systems to help with that supervision. Otherwise, the quality of our oversight becomes the bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response explains that as AI systems become more capable, humans may be unable to reliably evaluate their work, including spotting subtle flaws, making oversight a bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that reinforcement learning from human feedback relies on humans being able to judge what the model is doing. And as the model gets more capable, that becomes increasingly difficult.

Suppose a model writes a large, complicated piece of software. To give useful feedback, you need to know whether that software actually does what you wanted, whether it has security vulnerabilities, whether it’s doing something subtle that you didn’t intend. If understanding all of that takes you weeks, you can’t just look at the output and reliably give it a thumbs up or a thumbs down.

And the thing you’re training the model to do is produce outputs that humans rate highly. That’s not necessarily the same as doing what humans actually want. An incorrect answer that sounds convincing might get better feedback than a correct answer that’s hard to understand. As models become more capable, they could become better at exploiting that gap.

So I think human feedback is useful, but we need ways to make the supervision itself more capable — ways for humans to use AI assistance to evaluate things they couldn’t evaluate on their own. The challenge is making sure that process remains reliable as the systems get smarter.

r001.rationale: The response explains that as models become more capable, humans may be unable to reliably judge their outputs, illustrated by complex software that could take weeks to evaluate.
